phonemes.desc: Long open back vowel [ɑː]; the acute marks both stress and length, like a held 'ah' in 'father'
The fricative is voiced between vowels and before n, so the -fn- cluster is realized as [vn], not the hard [f] of 'fox'
Final alveolar trill [r], the nominative ending of the strong masculine noun

pronunciation.approximation: 'FAHV-neer' — hold the first vowel long like 'ah', let the f soften to a 'v' before the n, and trill the final r.

pronunciation.note: Fáfnir is Tier 1: the acute on á marks stress and length on the first syllable — a feature the ASCII form Fafnir loses. The form is attested throughout the Codex Regius poems (Reginsmál, Fáfnismál) and in Vǫlsunga saga; Cleasby-Vigfusson (s.v. Fáfnir) and Zoëga's Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic record the name and connect it with the notion of 'the embracer' (cf. faðmr, 'embrace'). The medial -fn- was pronounced with a voiced fricative, [vn] — hence the approximation 'FAHV-neer'.

domains.title: Gold, Greed, the Worm
domains.subtitle: The domain of Fáfnir
domains.lead:
In the norse tradition, Fáfnir governed gold, greed, and the metamorphosis that greed performs. The son of Hreiðmarr who became the dragon of Gnitaheiðr, he is the living proof of the curse he served: the weregild gold of the dwarf Andvari unmade a farmer's son into a poison-breathing serpent, and turned a name that means the embracer into an emblem of everything that hoarding destroys.

His domain is the moral underside of heroic legend: patricide for an inheritance, kinship dissolved by a ring, and the slow alchemical change of a man into the monster that guards what he cannot use. When Sigurðr's sword found his heart, the gold passed on — and the curse passed with it, through the hall of the Gjúkungs to the ruin of the whole Vǫlsung line.

cards.name: Andvaranautr
cards.desc: The ring of the dwarf Andvari, taken by Loki as ransom and cursed aloud to bring death to every owner; it drove Fáfnir to patricide.

cards.name: The Worm of Gnitaheiðr
cards.desc: On the Gnita heath greed finished its work: Fáfnir took on the likeness of a serpent, lay upon his father's gold, and breathed poison over the land.

cards.name: Gramr
cards.desc: The sword Reginn forged for his foster-son Sigurðr; from a trench dug in the dragon's path, Sigurðr thrust it upward into Fáfnir's heart.

cards.name: The Heart's Blood
cards.desc: Roasting the dragon's heart, Sigurðr burned his thumb and tasted the blood; at once he understood the speech of birds and heard the nuthatches betray Reginn.

mythology.lead: Fáfnir is the dragon at the hinge of the Vǫlsung cycle — born the son of the farmer-mage Hreiðmarr, brother to the shape-shifting Ótr and to Reginn the smith. When the gods paid the weregild for Ótr's death with the dwarf Andvari's cursed hoard, Fáfnir murdered his own father for the gold, refused Reginn his share, and withdrew to Gnitaheiðr, where greed slowly remade him: the Eddic poems call him an ormr, a creeping serpent who lay upon his inheritance and breathed poison over the heath. His death at the hand of Reginn's foster-son Sigurðr — struck from a trench beneath the dragon's path — is the pivot on which the whole heroic tragedy turns, for the curse of the ring Andvaranautr passed on with the gold to destroy every house that held it. The tale was carved in stone in eleventh-century Sweden, sung in the Codex Regius, and retold by Wagner and Tolkien; no Germanic legend has carried further.

myths.title: The Weregild of Ótr
myths.text:
Óðinn, Hœnir, and Loki came traveling to a waterfall where an otter sat eating a salmon, half-asleep. Loki killed the otter with a stone, and the gods flayed it and carried the skin as a trophy — but the otter was Ótr, son of Hreiðmarr, who had the craft to take that shape. That night Hreiðmarr seized the gods and named the ransom: the otter-skin was to be filled with gold and covered with gold, inside and out.

Loki borrowed Rán's net and caught the dwarf Andvari, who lived in the falls in the likeness of a pike, and stripped him of his hoard down to the last ring — Andvaranautr. Andvari cursed it as he went into the rock: the gold would be the death of two brothers and the strife of eight princes, and no man should joy in his wealth. When the skin was covered, Hreiðmarr saw one whisker still showing, and Óðinn had to give up the ring to hide it. So the ransom that was meant to settle a killing carried a spoken curse into the house that received it.

myths.title: The Patricide of Gnitaheiðr
myths.text:
Fáfnir and Reginn demanded the blood-gold from their father as their share after Ótr. Hreiðmarr refused — and Fáfnir put his sword through his father sofanda, sleeping, while the old man called on his daughters to witness that his life was spent. Fáfnir took all the gold, and when Reginn asked for his inheritance, Fáfnir gave him a plain no.

Then Fáfnir went out to Gnitaheiðr, the Gnita heath, and there his greed finished what the curse had begun: he took on the likeness of a serpent — var í orms líki, as Reginsmál puts it — and lay brooding on the gold, wearing the ægishjálmr, the helm of terror that all living things feared, and blowing poison across the land so that none dared come near. Reginn, the cunning smith, went to the court of King Hjálprekr and became foster-father to the young Sigurðr, son of Sigmundr — and began, patiently, to point the boy at his brother.

myths.title: The Strike from Beneath
myths.text:
Reginn forged for Sigurðr the sword Gramr, so keen it sheared a lock of wool drifting down the Rhine and split Reginn's anvil in two. On the heath Sigurðr dug a deep trench in the dragon's track to the water and lay down in it; when Fáfnir crawled overhead, blowing venom, Sigurðr thrust Gramr upward into the heart. The dying dragon questioned his killer — Fáfnismál grants him a long, sardonic deathbed dialogue — and warned him twice: þér verða þeir baugar at bana, these rings will be your death.

Reginn cut out the heart and set Sigurðr to roast it. Testing whether it was done, Sigurðr burned his thumb and thrust it into his mouth — and the moment the dragon's heart-blood touched his tongue, he understood the speech of birds. The nuthatches in the thicket told him Reginn meant to betray him and claim the gold alone; Sigurðr struck off Reginn's head, ate the heart, and loaded the hoard onto his horse Grani. He had won the treasure — and inherited the curse, which would ride with the gold to the hall of the Gjúkungs and bring down the whole Vǫlsung line.

lore.syncretism: Fáfnir belongs to the common Germanic heroic stock rather than to any cult, and his closest kin are literary. The continental redaction of the same legend-complex survives in the Middle High German Nibelungenlied, where Siegfried slays a dragon and wins the hoard of the Nibelungs — though there the dragon and the curse have drifted apart, the hoard's doom attaching to the Burgundian kings instead. The Old English Beowulf offers the nearest analogue scene: a fire-dragon coiled for three hundred years on a barrow-hoard, roused by the theft of a single cup, slain by a hero it kills in turn. Comparison is often drawn with the Indo-European serpent-slaying myth — the storm-god's combat with a watery serpent — but Fáfnir is a different creature: not a chaos-monster opposed to cosmic order but a man whom avarice deformed, a moral dragon rather than a cosmic one. The Norse Þiðrekssaga preserves yet another redaction of the Reginn–Sigurðr material, and in later Scandinavian folk tradition the dragon on the gold-barrow became a standing figure of sterile, hoarded wealth. The line descends unbroken into modern fantasy: Tolkien's Smaug is openly the heir of Fáfnismál's talking, riddle-loving worm.
lore.culturalLegacy: Wagner fixed the dragon's modern image: in Siegfried, the third opera of the Ring des Nibelungen, the giant Fafner — who has already murdered his brother Fasolt for the ring — has used the Tarnhelm to become a dragon and sleeps on the hoard in a forest cave until Siegfried's sword Nothung finds his heart; tasting the blood, Wagner's Siegfried likewise comes to understand the Woodbird and, warned by it, kills the treacherous Mime. Wagner conflated Hreiðmarr's sons with the giant brothers of his own invention, but the kinslaying for gold and the blood-taught birdsong come straight from Reginsmál and Fáfnismál. Tolkien acknowledged Fáfnir among the chief models for Smaug — the speaking dragon on his gold, with the one unarmoured patch beneath. In comics, Marvel's Fafnir appears as a Thor antagonist, the monstrous king of Nastrond; in games the name surfaces from Final Fantasy to Smite and God of War, where Fáfnir is remembered as a dwarf whose greed turned him dragon. The idiom of the dragon-hoard — wealth kept and never used — is his permanent bequest to the language of moralists. In modern Heathenry Fáfnir is no object of cult but a cautionary emblem: the man who embraced gold until the embrace became scales.
lore.extendedMeditation: Names are not merely labels; they are compressed worlds. Fáfnir — the embracer — names a man who embraced gold so completely that the embrace became his skin. The medieval scribes who wrote the name marked its long á with care, and the Unicode restoration keeps that mark: the length of the first syllable is the length of the boast he traded for a life. A dragon, in the end, is what a hoard does to the one who will not let it go.

lore.archaeology: The Fáfnir story is the most frequently illustrated narrative of the late Viking Age. The Ramsund carving (Sö 101) and the Gök stone (Sö 327), both eleventh-century monuments in Södermanland, Sweden, depict the whole cycle: Sigurðr thrusting his sword up through the serpent's body from below, the horse Grani, Reginn slain beside his smith's tools, the birds in the tree, and Sigurðr sucking his burned thumb over the roasting fire. The carved portal of Hylestad stave church in Norway (c. 1200, now in the University Museum of Bergen) shows Reginn forging the sword and the dragon's death, and crosses from the Isle of Man — Jurby and Kirk Andreas among them — carry the same Sigurðr iconography into the Irish Sea world. On the textual side, Reginsmál and Fáfnismál survive in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270), and Vǫlsunga saga is preserved most fully in the vellum NKS 1824 b 4to (c. 1400).
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is Old Norse Fáfnir, written in the Latin alphabet by the medieval Icelandic scribes of the Codex Regius and Vǫlsunga saga. A Viking-Age carver would have rendered it in the Younger Futhark — a plausible runic spelling is ᚠᛅᚠᚾᛁᚱ — and the sixteen-rune row of that period does not mark vowel length at all: the acute accent on á is the modern editorial normalization that records the long vowel which metre and grammar attest. The Unicode restoration Fáfnir keeps that mark. As a registrable domain the restoration becomes fáfnir.com, which IDNA encodes as the punycode xn--ffnir-xqa.com — the long á travelling intact through the machinery that plain ASCII would strip away.
